chat.said: We're a 15-person software agency. Clients keep asking us to host and maintain what we build for them. Should we start our own managed-hosting service, partner with an established hosting firm, or keep saying no? We want steady monthly revenue within a year without hurting delivery quality, and our engineers are already at about 85% utilisation.

answer.text: The comparison turns on who handles incidents, not who owns the servers. There is not yet enough evidence to distinguish the routes against both aims. Keeping saying no creates no hosting revenue; partnership only relieves delivery pressure if support responsibilities genuinely transfer.

why.text: Revenue chances remain unavailable because currency and commercial terms are unresolved

why.cite: The chance of 'Steady monthly revenue within a year' cannot be worked out yet: rests on "Positive recurring revenue threshold", which is not measured: Zero is the boundary between positive revenue and no revenue; its currency follows the revenue measure; rests on "Monthly hosting-related agency revenue", which is not measured: Recurring revenue received by the agency, not the hosting provider's total bill and not profit. Currency remains unresolved; rests on "Monthly agency revenue per paying client", which is not measured: No hosting offer produces no hosting-service revenue. Currency is unresolved rather than assumed.

why.text: The run applies hosting incident risk to declining despite excluding that exposure, so its quality result is not a sound comparison.

text.text: Map incident ownership and paid responsibilities across these routes to expose which would still interrupt project delivery.

chat.said: Candidate check set "Agency headcount" to 18 person.

answer.text: Agency headcount is now 18 people. That changes the agency total, not the engineering capacity used to compare hosting workloads, so it does not establish more room for hosting.

why.text: Engineering headcount remains Olumi’s staffing what-if, rather than your confirmed engineering capacity.

text.text: Check your staffing allocation for engineering full-time equivalents, excluding nonengineering roles. What engineering capacity does it show? This would test whether the hosting workload assumptions fit your team.

chat.said: Add a risk that two of our senior engineers leave within the year.

answer.text: The departure risk is now represented as lost engineering capacity, with project commitments unchanged and no replacement assumed. It does not capture lost senior review, client knowledge or handover work. The quality result for Keep saying no has changed from a calculated chance to unavailable because the run produced invalid values

answer.cite: The chance that 'Keep saying no' meets 'Without hurting delivery quality' is not worked out: in 4 draws a figure ('Deliveries accepted without corrective rework', 'Engineering capacity available after departures') went outside what it can be, such as below zero.

why.text: Departure timing and likelihood remain Olumi’s what-ifs, not your estimates.

text.text: Map which senior responsibilities would become uncovered and how cover could work, to distinguish replaceable capacity from delivery risks the model misses.
